speechtext:
1.	Did the RCMP request from the United States Immigration Service on or about April 13, 1980, licence numbers on Canadian pleasure boats tied up at Morristown, N.Y. docks or anywhere within a reasonable distance of the area and, if so, for what reason and specifically, was it because of the alleged failure of certain Canadians, stopping for dinner in the United States while cruising the river, to report to Canadian Customs on return to Canada and, if so, how many Canadians were assessed penalties by the RCMP in the area of Brockville, Ontario for such an offence and was the penalty $50 in each case?
2.	Is the government aware that the U.S. government has a system whereby Americans can obtain a seasonal permit for similar crossings to the Canadian side of the border without reporting in on return unless they have goods to declare and specifically, will the government consider the institution of a similar permit system for Canadians in order to eliminate the present problem?
3.	(a) In regard to this particular type of matter, is RCMP action taken under the Canada Customs Act and, if so (i) for what reason does the RCMP not have to offer evidence against a person before a penalty is levied (ii) is a person considered guilty until they can prove their innocence (b) will the government consider amendments to the Canada Customs Act to provide seasonal permits and to permit persons to be considered innocent until proven guilty by a court?

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: PLEASURE BOATS-CANADIAN CUSTOMS SEASONAL PERMITS
speechtext:
I am informed by the Ministry of the Solicitor General and the Department of National Revenue as follows: 1. The RCMP have had no contact with the U.S. Immigration Service concerning licence numbers of Canadian boats in U.S. waters.
As a result of complaints by Canadian Customs officers that Canadians travelling via boat to the U.S.A. were not reporting to customs on their return to Canada, RCMP members contacted U.S. Customs officials on or about April 13, 1980, requesting licence numbers of Canadian boats found in U.S. ports. The reason for the request was to confirm inward report

April 2, 1981
Order Paper Questions
to Canadian Customs. A total of 19 Canadians were assessed penalties by the RCMP in the area of Brockville, Ontario for such an offence and the penalty was $50 in each case.
2.	It is understood that United States regulations have the following requirements. All pleasure boats, regardless of size, need not report to U.S. Immigration when arriving with only U.S. citizens on board. However, all vessels must comply with customs reporting and entry requirements. In this regard, an American pleasure boat owned by a U.S. citizen must report arrival from a foreign area to customs within 24 hours. The report may be made by any means of communication, and if inspection is required, customs will direct the vessel to an inspection area.
Under the Canadian system, all persons arriving in Canada are also required to report to customs. The reporting mechanism varies from region to region according to the traffic volume, distances between offices, and availability of customs personnel. In some areas, officers are on duty at all locations during the season to process marine traffic, while in other areas, the system is complemented by the use of telephone reporting procedures. In areas where telephone procedures are used, residents of Canada may pre-register with Canada Customs before travelling on international waters. In all cases, however, a customs report is required in respect of each trip. As with the U.S. system, the traveller may be given a verbal clearance by customs and issued a clearance number, or may be required to wait on board pending inspection by a customs officer.
3.	(a) The action taken by the RCMP was under the
provisions of the Customs Act.
(i)	The RCMP officers offered evidence to the above mentioned 19 persons that a Customs Act violation was believed to have taken place. All persons admitted being in the U.S.A. and not reporting to customs.
(ii)	Under section 248 of the Customs Act, burden of proof lies on the person whose duty it was to comply with the act. However, RCMP investigators must have sufficient grounds to prove the offence has taken place before taking any action.
(b) The Department of National Revenue will consider amendments to the Customs Act to ensure the latitude exists for the establishment of various reporting procedures according to the circumstances and conditions in each region.
It is a cornerstone of our legal system that a person charged with a crime is presumed to be innocent until proven guilty and this principle will not be changed. However, it is important to realize that the question of guilt or innocence only arises under the Customs Act when criminal charges have been laid. In most instances where action is taken under the Customs Act, civil proceedings are involved. In these cases, it is the goods in Canada which have not been reported to customs that are in violation of the law, and action is directed
against the goods in question and not the person in possession of them. The action is considered to be "in rem". The innocence or guilt of the person involved does not therefore arise in such cases.

Definitions
Domiciliary Care
"Domiciliary Care", as used in DVA, equates to federal types I and II care. A domiciliary care patient is reasonably well and ambulatory; is capable of looking after his or her own needs; is able to get up, get dressed and go to the dining room; requires a minimum of either nursing or medical care or other assistance, and is essentially being provided with board and quarters.
Chronic Care
Chronic Care, which is federal type III care, is that required by a person who is chronically ill and/or has a functional disability (physical or mental) whose acute phase of illness is over, whose initial processes may or may not be stable, whose potential for rehabilitation may be limited, and who requires a range of therapeutic services, medical management and skilled nursing care plus provision for meeting psycho-social needs. The period of time during which care is required is unpredictable, but usually consists of a matter of months or years.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL SALES TAX REMISSION ON BUILDING MATERIALS
speechtext:
1.	Is a general formula in use for calculating the amount of federal sales tax remission on building materials, for example, new schools and hospitals and, if so, what is it?
2.	What are the guidelines or regulations pertaining to the rebate of federal sales taxes in Part 1 ?

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude Tessier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: FEDERAL SALES TAX REMISSION ON BUILDING MATERIALS
speechtext:
1. A general formula or simplified method, as mentioned below, may be used to compute the refund of federal sales tax on materials used exclusively in the construction of a building for a hospital or a school.
2. Hospitals
An institution certified as a bona fide public hospital by the Department of National Health and Welfare claims sales tax exemption at the time of purchase or importation of building materials for its own use and not for sale. Accordingly, a hospital making direct purchases for a building construction program can obtain materials tax exempt and make the goods available to the general contractor or subcontractor. Or, the hospital may grant the contractor or subcontractor or both authority to purchase materials exempt on its behalf. A contractor or subcontractor who has not been appointed the hospital's purchasing agent is required to pay tax at the time of purchase and claim a refund from the Department of National Revenue. The refund may be computed either by claiming the exact amount of sales tax as substantiated by suppliers' invoices or by using a simplified method and calculating the tax as 2.25 per cent of the total contract payments.
Schools
Unlike a hospital, a school must pay sales tax when purchasing or importing materials for use in the construction of a building. However, the school may obtain reimbursement of the tax by filing for a refund based on either the exact amount of sales tax as substantiated by suppliers' invoices or by using a simplified method. In
Order Paper Questions
this instance the tax factor is 1.5 per cent of the total contract payments less an allowance for provincial tax (in Ontario .0315 per cent) for a net of 1.4685 per cent.
The tax factor is lower for a school than for a hospital because a hospital is entitled to an exemption on all goods it purchases whereas a school is entitled to a refund only on materials for use in the construction of a building. For instance, a fence around a school is subject to sales tax.

We have all the ingredients we need to be self-sufficient and we have the human and physical resources to achieve greatness in the world community of nations, but not by borrowing. We have access to petroleum reserves and every known mineral in the world, many of them in abundance. We have rich farmland, the fisheries, all the wherewithal to meet our domestic requirements and then some, if we stop borrowing. We have the capacity to become one of the manufacturing giants of the world. We have the capacity to become one of the world's great exporting nations. Instead, we have not begun to exploit our enormous potential.
We are still hewers of wood and drawers of water. Much of our export trade is raw or semi-processed resources. We find ourselves in the ludicrous position of exporting our raw resources to other countries and then ending up buying them back in the form of fully finished manufactured or processed products. It is being done by borrowing.
For a decade the government has paid lip service to industrial strategy and research and development. With this government, if I may paraphrase Lewis Carroll in "Through the Looking Glass", it is always "jam yesterday and jam tomorrow but never jam today".
Let us just look for a minute at expenditures on research and development. My colleague in the House of Commons and my party's spokesman for research and development, the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. Gilchrist), has just issued a special report on R and D. We currently spend less than 1 per cent, .94 per cent to be exact, of the gross national product on research and development. We borrow to do everything else. My colleague's expert sources tell him that for every one half of 1 per cent of the gross national product spent on research, 400,000 jobs are created. That is what we are talking about: jobs, inflation, the economy, not borrowing. That expenditure by the government would cut unemployment by 50 per cent in this country.
Research and development investment increases of 1.5 per cent or 2 per cent could eliminate unemployment. I am a businessman. I operate a small wholesale business in Barrie, Ontario, which has been in business since 1892. Our annual sales are in excess of $15 million. I will tell you, as a businessman, I am appalled at the way the government is mismanaging this country. We are running harder to stand still. Our manufacturing sector is overtaxed, overregulated and is not in a position to compete with the industrial plants of other nations. Those are the hard facts and it is getting worse and worse as we continue this borrowing madness.
We can turn it all around. The idea is not to be negative but positive. But the longer the government keeps its head in the sand, the longer it will take us to catch up with the rest of the world. We should never have been placed in the position of playing catch-up ball by a huge deficit and by more and more borrowing.
Look at what is happening in the rest of the world. Last year I had the good fortune of visiting Japan. In 1980, Japan

They did not do it by borrowing. The Japanese have long since overtaken and passed the United States in television and radio production. Japanese steel plants have the same capacity as the United States and almost as much as the European Common Market.
Three years ago, Japanese investment in new plant and equipment equalled that of the United States, but listen to this-with half the population, the per capita investment was twice that of the United States, and this did not happen by borrowing. In the early eighties, Japan will surpass the United States in total research and development.
Very soon Japan will be a world leader in computers, motorcycles, machine tools, copying machines and snowmobiles. Does anyone in this House think there is any reason why Canada could not do the same with our economy if we stopped borrowing?
I see my time is almost up. Let me conclude by saying that if we were to obtain large quantities of investment dollars, Canada would have to employ the same techniques that are used in other countries. We could do that with a lot of other vehicles, such as profit sharing.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) made a very good point when he said that perhaps it is about time the rules were revamped so as not to have to go the 75c route. I agree with that. I think the House leader of our party agrees with it, and I certainly hope that during the life of this Parliament we can come to grips with it. In the meantime we have not been able to come to grips with anything for some weeks. We must set a reasonable time limit so as to be able to come to grips with this bill and borrow the money which is in fact necessary to keep the government going.
I was interested in the comments of the hon. member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart) who was talking about borrowing, how he is opposed to borrowing, does not like it and thinks we should not be doing it. I am not sure anybody is wild about it, but the fact of the matter is that when his party was in power briefly, the deficit was not decreased. We heard a lot of predictions prior to that party assuming power, that in fact when it got into office the deficit would decrease immediately. That did not happen. I remember the day when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) said he had come to the conclusion, in fact, that the deficit would perhaps have to go up but this would be a short-term measure and, hopefully, after a reasonable period of time they would be able to turn things around and start a shrinking deficit, reducing the requirement for borrowing. That certainly was what was supposed to happen in terms of an increased deficit in the budget of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). That is exactly what did happen.
It is not as though suddenly you can somehow push a button, wave a magic wand and the need for borrowing disappears. There are some facts of life, and one of them is that before we are in a position to eliminate borrowing, we will have to continue to borrow if in fact the process of government is to continue. That is what we have to do. It is with regret we are in the position where we have no choice but to use the provisions of 75c to bring this to a head and get on with it, but that is the position we are in.
In the last few days, since March 24, there have been well over 100 points of order and questions of privilege, virtually all

of which have been frivolous and spurious. In fact, the House leader of the official opposition indicated they were prepared to waste the time of Parliament. I was sitting opposite when he used that phrase. I sort of had the feeling he immediately knew he has said something like C. D. Howe when he said, "what's a million", or something like Walter Harris when he said, "the six-buck boys". It just gets out and you wish somehow you could pull that word back in or that you had not used it. He did say that. He said they were prepared to deliberately waste the time of Parliament. If there is one thing on which I am prepared to congratulate the opposition House leader it is his honesty on that occasion. He was very honest because that is what they have been doing for some time, and, regrettably, that is what they continue to do.
I sense a better mood in the House today. I hope we may be reaching the point where we can come to some agreement on the impasse which has held Parliament up to ransom. "Hijacked Parliament" is a phrase that has been used, and I think that is accurate. It is unfortunate we are in this situation, but we have to get on with the governing of the country. We must pass this borrowing bill, and we are using Standing Order 75c, not in any improper way, as was suggested a few minutes ago, but in accordance with the Standing Orders in a quite proper, reasonable and legitimate way. This is a custom which has developed in recent years. I do not believe we forced the government of that party opposite to do that when we were in opposition, but it is something that has become the custom in recent years. I think it is quite within my right to discuss procedural matters in connection with Bill C-59, the borrowing authority. That is the reason I was making the comments I was making, following on the comments by the hon. member for Don Valley East and my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. This is a procedural motion. It does not necessarily deal with the substance of the borrowing bill. What we have to explain to the people out there, members of the House and those who read Hansard, is why the government is limiting debate at this particular stage.
I was about to say that the reason we are doing this is that the affairs of the nation must be conducted in fairness, yes, but with some expediency. The government has an obligation, and I know members on the other side decry this. This government was elected to govern the country. It was elected to put before Parliament legislation to deal with the governing of this nation. It is an obligation of the government to see that its legislative program gets through Parliament using, of course, the proper parliamentary means at its disposal. The motion under 75a, b and c was developed about 11 or 12 years ago as a means to speed up debate. We in this country have almost a gun-shyness about using any allocation of time motion. We are faced today with the fact that our rules are somewhat archaic, but in today's modern society when fast decisions are required, when inflation, unemployment, and exchange problems all face Canadians, Parliament must act as best it can.
I submit that we need a major overhaul of our rules. One of those overhauls took place 11 or 12 years ago and the development of the time allocation motion which is now before us this evening was adopted. It is a means on which agreement cannot be achieved. And agreement could not be achieved in this case. I was present at those meetings, as is called for in the Standing Orders, when agreement under Standing Order 75a and 75c was not possible on report stage and third reading of Bill C-59. Therefore, it is perfectly within the rights of the government to proceed in this fashion.
Now, in Great Britain, the Mother of all Parliaments, Westminster-which has been cited this week as a substantial basis for the positions of those arguing points of order concerning the constitutional debate-is much more efficient than we are. Second reading of a bill passes within one sitting. That sitting may last until six o'clock in the morning, but it is of one day's duration. Mr. Speaker, how much debate is required to state whether one or one's party is or is not in favour of a piece of legislation before the House? So I think that the use of the time allocation rule 75c is quite defensible.

My good friend, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) rose in this House to move a motion under Standing Order 75c on Bill C-20, which was the infamous Conservative property tax credit then before the House. I believe it was at Committee of the Whole stage. He talked in terms of this not being closure, of it being time allocation, a far gentler measure. And he said, quite rightly so because he was in government at the time, that the government has a certain responsibility when all positions have been made known, when everybody has expressed their opinion, to actually force the debate to an end and force the question.
I do not want to stray because I know that tempers have perhaps flared in the past few days, but I submit there is an analogy between the time allocation we are proposing on this borrowing bill and the time allocation discussion on the Constitution. I will not belabour that point, but I want our friends in the country watching us tonight, and members on the other side, to realize that this is no nefarious scheme to gag Parliament, this is purely a fair and efficient manner of disposing of the government's legislative program. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) stated earlier this year that he was not embarrassed to use the time allocation motion, and I quite agree with him. I think my colleagues on this side agree. It is up to the Canadian public to actually make the final decision as to whether or not the government is indeed cutting off debate and doing it in an unfair manner.
When this was done in 1956, the government of the day fell because, with all due respect to the fact that it was a Liberal government, Standing Order 43, which is not what is applied tonight, was used, but not in the most judicious manner. So it is not the rule that matters but how it is applied, whether there is not only a semblance and appearance but actual fairness in any debate terminated, whether by time allocation or by closure. I hate to mention that because closure is almost a four letter word, it is almost unparliamentary. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission, my comments will be about the use of Standing Order 75c and the need to reform the rules of the House rather than about the bill in respect of which the order is being used.
During the Thirtieth Parliament, the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization studied the question of reform of the rules of the House. Unfortunately, there was no action at the time in spite of much good will and hard work by members on all sides of the House. One particular proposition which received a good deal of attention at that time was the suggestion that, at the second reading stage, which is approval in principle, the debate be limited to one day and that the major debate on a bill should occur at third reading, after the committee has made whatever amendments seem appropriate following the hearing of witnesses. This is a proposal which I hope will be considered again and, perhaps, acted on shortly in this session.
What happens now at second reading stage is that we tend to have lengthy speeches. A long speech is not necessarily designed to be persuasive, to advance an argument or increase understanding. We have long speeches at second reading. We have the same points discussed in committee, again at report stage and again at third reading. I think members on all sides of the House suffer from this process because when fewer members can participate, both supporters of the government and members of the opposition feel frustrated. They do not feel the same sense of commitment toward dealing with the business of the House in an orderly fashion.
In the case of the bill before us, the borrowing authority, there were five days of debate at second reading before 75c was introduced, since it was not possible to reach an agreement to limit debate in any way. We then had another two days of debate after 75c was moved. This is a practice which seems to be taking place so often with our bills.
Recently I came across a definition of "nation" in St. Augustine's "the City of God" which read as follows:
A nation is an association of reasonable beings united in a peaceful sharing of the things they cherish.
I know many members of the opposition share that view. Very often when we work on committee, we are able to subordinate our partisan differences and work in a constructive fashion. We can expose our differences, but we do it with the intention of arriving at some common ground. Certainly as Canadians, when an all-party delegation goes abroad, usually we are able to agree among ourselves that we will present honestly our differences of opinion based on our different ideologies, but also, in the national interest, we try to present a reasonable picture of the things upon which we agree as Canadians.
What has been happening to the nation's business in recent days has been dispiriting. There has been a lot of name-calling which has been unsophisticated and unseemly. These have not been the highest days in the history of Parliament. While structural changes such as changes in the rules of the House will not solve all these problems, I think they would assist. With shorter speeches, with more work done in committee, with more opportunities for all of us to participate, we could reduce a lot of the unnecessary irritants in the House. We will always have differences of principle and differences of opinion, but it is urgent that we try to reduce some of the unnecessary irritants.
The eighteenth century definition that the role of opposition is "to oppose" is surely very old-fashioned for us. Surely, what is needed in our time is much more opportunity for members of the opposition and supporters of the government to work constructively together, recognizing some basic differences, and to be prepared occasionally to make more than a normal effort to find middle ground.
One of the big changes I should like to see, whenever we get around to discussing the rules of the House seriously, is a change in the rules of question period. In Westminster, sup-
April 2, 1981

porters of the government can ask questions, just as members of the opposition can. In this House there has been a tradition that question period is the prerogative of the opposition. I think three Speakers have held that supporters of the government are able to get information in other ways. This is true, but I think our constituents have a right to see us representing their interests publicly; they should not always have to depend on faith and assume that we are pursuing their interests in caucus. It should be possible for those who have elected supporters of the government to see us expressing our concern for the interests of our constituents in exactly the same manner as members of the opposition can.
So, these are some of the issues which I trust will be addressed soon in Parliament. I know all members of the House would like to see some changes in the rules of the House which would enable us all to do our jobs more effectively and hopefully would reduce the number of occasions when Standing Order 75c or similar motions would have to be called into play.

Mr. Speaker, I am torn between a feeling of satisfaction and a feeling of bitterness. That satisfaction stems from the fact that we in the House can talk with so much ease and abandon about billions of dollars without giving the odd thought to the fact that there are people in our country who have hardly a few cents to live or survive.
That satisfaction is due, of course, to the possibility we as, Canadians have to own huge untapped resources which make it possible for us to use that borrowing power almost at will. But using that borrowing authority does involve some risks. Indeed we must never forget that we ought to show a lot more moderation when borrowing because we have to keep in mind that the money we borrow will sooner or later be paid back by the people, by the taxpayers and, especially, by the workers.
Mr. Speaker, I think I am speaking for the workers in my riding as well as others throughout the country when I say that taxes now weigh heavily on that class of citizens who never miss an opportunity to tell us that their pay cheque has a long list of deductions and precious little left in the way of income. I think that the debate this evening should make us pause for a moment, because if in today's world we have made commitments toward our people and must respect them by adopting the bill before us, we must still think about the future and ask ourselves how one day we will have to use more sparingly the money we can get so easily.
I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that I had mixed feelings of both satisfaction and bitterness. My bitterness stems from the atmosphere in this House. I have a feeling that every time the government introduces a bill, the speakers almost always feel obliged to attack, in a way that strikes me as exaggerated, the hon. members who try to represent as best they can the interests of the taxpayers.
I feel our hon. friends opposite should realize that we are not borrowing such enormous amounts for the fun of it. We have obligations to meet. We also have people who are entitled to a
April 2, 1981

minimum of comfort, and we must protect the interests of the underprivileged in our society. When I see what language is too often used in this House by some hon. members, I wonder if we are aware of the example we should set for the population as a whole, namely, that of parliamentarians who are eager to work for the good of all the people rather than for the promotion of a political and partisan philosophy.
Mr. Speaker, I listened very closely to the speeches that were made and I must say that my comments do not apply to all parliamentarians; but it does seem to me that we should be mature enough and wise enough in debates of this type, when we discuss before the whole nation matters as important as those before the House this evening, to address our remarks to the real issues instead of attacking the persons who either defend or oppose them. I believe I echo the statements of several hon. members when I deplore the fact that we have to resort to setting time limits for our debates. And I have no intention of saying that the opposition is solely responsible for this situation, even if it contributes to it. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that if we, as parliamentarians, want to convince the population that politicians are able to disregard party lines in their search for real solutions to our problems, if we want to convince the population that parliamentarians and politicians are mature people as they claim to be, then it becomes more and more necessary to find solutions which will allow us to schedule the proceedings of this House so as to discuss a bit more calmly such important questions which affect the wellbeing of our fellow citizens.
Mr. Speaker, when we talk about billions of dollars in this House, we are often tempted to forget that the real problem is not the borrowing itself, but rather how the money will be used to benefit those who really need it. The wish I express this evening, Mr. Speaker, is that when these sums are voted, we take greater care to ensure that they are used for the benefit of those who need it most. We are too much inclined to believe, Mr. Speaker, that everyone in Canada is wealthy and well off, while the facts show that this is not so, Mr. Speaker, and that even in a country with as many dynamic and able people as ours, there are also poor people who are often ignored and who would require the co-operation and the assistance of parliamentarians.
This evening, Mr. Speaker, I would like to appeal to all my colleagues on both sides of the House to spare a thought, while dealing with all those millions of dollars, for the poor, for the disadvantaged, and for those who expect us to make a conciliatory gesture of support and assistance. I trust, Mr. Speaker, that the funds which we shall agree to spend in the next few months and weeks will be used for the benefit of those who need it most.

I am not going to argue the merits of the opposition of that party. I am only saying that kind of activity will lead to more restrictive rules and regulations rather than to more openness which we ought to have here.
It worries me when we are required to have time allocation brought in. Call it time allocation, call it closure, it does not matter. They mean the same. The debate will end at a time predetermined by the government. It flies in the face of parliamentary tradition, as I understand and like to think of it. Parliamentary tradition tells me that the government will propose to Parliament the legislation that it hopes to pass and that Parliament will dispose of that legislation having reasoned it through, offered its suggestions, and ultimately will support or defeat it. In that kind of co-operative House, time allocation measures such as this would never be necessary.
I think there is a misunderstanding here of the roles. The government has a right to expect to be given the latitude and leeway it requires in order to govern, but it does not have the right to muzzle the opposition whenever it feels so inclined. I want to suggest that the behaviour of the opposition from time to time arouses the passions and the anger of the government, and it will respond, just as the behaviour of the government will arouse the passions and anger of the opposition and it will respond. However, those occasions must never be allowed to become the main feature of the parliamentary system and the main impetus for negative change to the rules.
I am sure that when people sent us here, they believed we had reached a stage of adult growth, a degree of native intelligence, an understanding of the process, a commitment to the country and that we were capable of representing the many

If nothing else, there has to be an informal working group sitting together on a regular basis to look at the rules, consult with the Speaker, Deputy Speaker and Acting Speakers, consult with the Table officers and the House leaders, to try and come up with a comprehensive program for change which will allow Parliament to work and enable us to have the kind of timetabling procedures without being faced with the time-wasting procedures which this motion in fact is. We could run into this again and the government could be in bad financial straits and have to delay a borrowing authority bill into a fiscal year for which there was no borrowing authority. I think the $3 billion non-lapsing flexibility is the kind of thing which should be provided for automatically, especially if we move to a new budgetary cycle. I suggest we should do that. The Minister of Finance has indicated that is what he would like to do. I refer to a fall budgetary cycle, bringing the budget forward in the fall. This would mean that the borrowing authority bill could not be brought in until probably December, or perhaps January. This makes a relatively tight legislative time frame within which to bring forward a borrowing authority bill, get it through second reading, into committee, back for report stage, third reading and royal assent after going through the Senate as well. We are talking about a very tight fiscal time-frame in which to get the borrowing authority bill through.
It makes sense to have a fall budgetary cycle for many reasons. One is that having your budgets in the late fall would allow the provinces to see what the federal fiscal framework will look like and, therefore, plan their budgets more effectively, and, typically, they come in the spring. In fact, we have had very good reaction from the provinces in respect of that kind of a suggestion at the December meeting of finance ministers. We were discussing when they would like to see a federal budget and the kind of consultation and interaction they would like between the two levels of government in order that budgetary cycles of all governments could be more closely integrated with better co-ordination than we have now. I think that is a good process.
In doing this, as I said, it does place the federal government in a rather peculiar situation, having a very short time-span from the point at which the budget is brought down to the fiscal year end when new borrowing authority has to be implemented. As a result, this non-lapsing component of the
current borrowing authority bill gives us flexibility if contingencies occur so the bill cannot be brought forward, as in the event of an election, for example, which was the case on February 18, 1980. That did not allow the fiscal framework and borrowing authority bill to be brought in immediately. Last year we had to go in fact until June or July before we could bring in a borrowing authority bill. For all these reasons I think it is a good thing for the government.
I think if the government changed, hon. members opposite would say exactly the same thing. They were very happy, I am sure, to have had that non-lapsing borrowing authority provided for in the previous budget so they could carry on the fiscal operations of government without having to call Parliament, rush a borrowing authority bill through before having a notion as to what their fiscal requirements were to be and what kind of financial plans they wanted to make. I think that non-lapsing authority is an extremely valuable component of a borrowing authority bill.
Also in respect of the bill we are bringing forward I would like to say a few more words. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to discuss this important motion before the House under Standing Order 75c. This government is attempting to tell us that this is simply an allocation of time, that it is not closure motion and was never intended to be such. In actual fact, if one reads what the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) said when he moved this motion, he will see the motion, as reported at page 8830 of Hansard for March 31 states the following:
-for the purpose of this order and, in turn, every question then necessary in order to dispose of the stage of the bill then under consideration shall be put forthwith and successively, without further debate or amendment.
The "Oxford Illustrated Dictionary" defines closure in Parliament as a decision by vote of the House of Commons to put a question without further debate.
Members of the government are attempting to tell us that this is simply an allocation of time. Like many other things that happen in the House, they say one thing and do another.
I should like to take you back to the 1969 debate when Mr. Blair, who was in charge of the committee which brought in 75c stated, as reported at page 10957 of Hansard for July 8:
I would like to say first of all with reference to Standing Order 75c that it cannot be invoked unilaterally by the government.
I should like to know how it is being invoked if it is not being invoked unilaterally. It is binding on our side and not binding on the government. Only the government can bring it
in.
Now, Mr. Speaker, they are telling us it is an allocation of time. But here we have a bill for $14 billion which the
April 2, 1981

government wishes to pass, and they want to allocate the minimum amount of time for debate. I would like to quote Mr. Blair, the chairman of that committee in 1969 when he said:
I think what I have said is clearly on record.
There will be at least ten days of time in this debate. Well, Mr. Speaker, there has not been ten days of time in this debate. He also said that there would be at least three days of debate in committee, and there were only two days of debate in committee. We can go on and on, but this is not allocation of time, it is just another method of closure.
What do they really want to do? They want to borrow $14 billion when we know that as of March 26 they had $6.4 billion. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) admitted that they still had $4.8 billion, which means they spent $1.6 billion in one week. The Minister of Finance admitted in committee that the government needs approximately $1 billion a month more than they receive. Why do they need to borrow $14 billion when they have $4.8 billion left? And at the rate at which they admitted they were spending more than they were taking in, they only need $1 billion. So it is quite obvious that this government does not know what they are spending.
I would like to quote the Minister of Finance further. He said five months ago that inflation was going to be 10 per cent, and admitted last week that it was 12.2 per cent. When did he have that revelation? Obviously he did not know five months ago, yet the deputy governor of the Bank of Canada admitted in committee that they are able to define inflation six months ahead. How come the Bank of Canada knew we were going to have 12 per cent inflation but the Minister of Finance did not? He still does not know. He does not know what inflation is going to be next month.
This government does not need the $14 billion it wishes to borrow; it is a sham. If it needed the money, we would be more than happy to pass it the bill, but it is quite obvious that the minister admitted they did not yet need to borrow the money. But, he says, one of these days they will.
In conclusion, there is no need to impose Standing Order 75c. This government brought it in in 1969 to limit debate and it is just another way that this government is going to close off debate, and that is why over the last week we have been attempting to bring this government to order so that they will be responsible for what they are doing.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO LIMIT REPORT STAGE AND THIRD READING DEBATE ON BORROWING AUTHORITY BILL
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MOTION TO LIMIT REPORT STAGE AND THIRD READING DEBATE ON BORROWING AUTHORITY BILL
speechtext:
And we are not going to allow this government to get away with spending money irrationally, we are not going to allow them to get away with imposing on this country an illegal and irrational resolution to the British Parliament. And we are going to continue to stand and speak against this government on bill after bill until they get sick and tired of trying to impose closure, whether it be Standing Order 75c or Standing Order 33. We do not intend to let this government get away with it any more. We have reached the point where we are not going to allow this government to run roughshod over the opposition.
Time Limitation

subsubtopic: MOTION TO LIMIT REPORT STAGE AND THIRD READING DEBATE ON BORROWING AUTHORITY BILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always with great pleasure and honour that I rise to speak in this House, all the more so because the subject we are debating tonight is very important for our country. As it has been done regularly over the past few years, we have to borrow billions of dollars for the day to day affairs of the state. Oftentimes that money goes to the poorest Canadians, those who benefit from the redistribution of wealth. It is precisely because they need it without delay that we are here debating this bill tonight.
I should like to be more specific and refer to the fact that we had to set a limit on this debate. It is true that when Canada borrows $13 billion for its regular budget the people are entitled to know why and, normally, it is a good subject for debate. But there has been an allocation of time for this debate; the reasons for that are not all that complicated and I can explain in a few words. This time allocation is due to the fact that over the past two weeks the Progressive Conservative party has resorted to all kinds of tricks, a sort of organized disorder of nothing but points of order and questions of privilege in the House with the result that we have been unable to do our job in the last 15 days. That is why we set a limit on the debate.
Organized disorder cannot be tolerated in a rink when people play hockey, or on a football field, and much less in the House, and in such a situation, we have to hurry in the last minutes to accomplish what we have to do. That is what is happening now. Still, no matter how bad things are, there is always a positive aspect. It is true that since we have been witnessing this organized disorder, we have seen a lot more Progressive Conservative members across the floor, a very rare event. I can say that it does change the panorama, for instead of seeing five or ten of our colleagues we can now see 50 of them or even more at the same time. I would not say it is an honour, but it is a more pleasing sight than empty benches.
In that same line of thought, I would like to point out that when our government borrows $13 billion, there are people who talk about blank cheques or what have you, but that is not what is happening at all. The simple fact is that because Canada collects taxes at specific times of the year, the government sometimes does not have enough money to carry on its routine business, to redistribute wealth in the country so that those most disadvantaged are a little less unfortunate and at least keep their human dignity.
This is precisely what we are doing with this borrowing. We are simply getting the money that the government needs to fulfil the commitments made by its predecessors, whether they were Progressive Conservatives or Liberals, to the citizens of this country. Obviously, when we can have the co-operation of the official opposition, this becomes much easier and can be accomplished in better conditions. We have been living in the last two weeks in the organized disorder of a party which should be progressive, but seems to be increasingly conserva-

tive. Since we have been living in these conditions, we have had to take the bull by the horns, as we often say in the Lake Saint-Jean area, and limit the duration of this debate. Those who benefit most from this will obviously be the Canadian people because the Government of Canada, which is their government, will be able to meet its commitments to them and continue to help them develop their resources in this vast and beautiful country which is very important for all of us. It is in this context that we are taking this action. I hope that our friends in the Progressive Conservative Party will understand why we are limiting this debate. I also hope that they will acquire some wisdom in the process, which will be useful in another important debate which has been going on for sometime in the House, a wisdom which is quite Canadian, very little conservative, extremely progressive, which goes beyond narrow partisanship, strictly inspired by political motives. May the Divine Light guide them very strongly so that they will understand-
